chosen_title: Astronomers discover Earth's new 'next-door neighbor' — a potentially habitable planet
caption:
🪐 A potentially livable planet was just found 25 light-years away — and astronomers are calling it 'exciting.'

A team of astronomers, including researchers at UC Irvine, has discovered a planet orbiting inside its star's habitable zone just 25 light-years from Earth. The habitable zone is the orbital sweet spot where conditions could theoretically allow liquid water to exist on a planet's surface — the first and most critical box scientists check when hunting for life beyond Earth.

For perspective: the celebrated TRAPPIST-1 system — home to the most famous cluster of potentially Earth-sized planets — sits roughly 40 light-years away. At 25 light-years, this newly found neighbor is significantly closer, and its proximity makes it one of the best candidates yet for telescopes like James Webb to scan for atmospheric gases that could point toward biological activity.

Why it matters: Every nearby candidate like this shrinks the search for life from 'somewhere in the infinite universe' to 'that specific star, right there.' The closer it is, the better our chances of actually learning something real.

Source: Space.com / New York Post (UC Irvine research)

slides.headline: Everyone assumed the nearest habitable planet was impossibly far. It isn't.

slides.label: THE STORY
slides.headline: A planet. 25 light-years away. Potentially livable.
slides.body: Astronomers — including researchers at UC Irvine — have discovered a planet sitting just 25 light-years from Earth that orbits inside its star's habitable zone, the region where liquid water could theoretically exist on a surface. Scientists described the find as 'exciting,' and the numbers back that up: 25 light-years is one of the shortest distances ever recorded for a potentially habitable world. For comparison, the famous TRAPPIST-1 system — home to several Earth-sized habitable-zone planets — sits roughly 40 light-years away, making this new neighbor significantly closer to home.

slides.label: HOW IT WORKS
slides.art_prompt: A cartoon cosmic map drawn like a cozy suburban neighborhood directory: Earth's sun sits at the top of a starry street with a tiny mailbox and a bright 'YOU ARE HERE' lawn flag, and just a short block of darkness away, a warm blue-green planet nestles in front of a small orange star with a hand-painted 'HABITABLE ZONE' welcome banner strung above it like a shop sign — the two worlds looking almost close enough to wave at each other across the dark.
slides.headline: The Goldilocks zone, explained
slides.body: The habitable zone is the orbital distance from a star that is not too hot and not too cold — the precise range where liquid water could pool on a planet's surface. It is the single most important first filter in the search for life beyond Earth.

slides.label: THE NUMBER
slides.caption: Light-years from Earth to our newly discovered potentially habitable neighbor. Most confirmed habitable-zone exoplanets sit hundreds to thousands of light-years away — making this one of the closest candidates ever found.

slides.label: WHY IT MATTERS
points: At just 25 light-years, this planet is closer to Earth than the celebrated TRAPPIST-1 system at roughly 40 light-years, making it one of the nearest potentially habitable worlds ever confirmed.

Being in the habitable zone does not guarantee life — it means liquid water could theoretically survive on the surface, which is the first and most critical condition scientists require before investigating further.

The planet's proximity makes it an exceptional target for the James Webb Space Telescope, which can analyze the atmospheres of nearby worlds for gases like oxygen or methane that might hint at biological processes.
UC Irvine researchers called the discovery 'exciting' — unusually strong language in academic astronomy, where cautious understatement is very much the norm.
